tip: Rectus means straight: this pair runs straight up and down beside the midline. Tendinous bands cross it, which is what makes the six-pack look.
The outermost flank muscle, with fibers running down and in like hands slipped into front pockets.
Sits just under the outer flank muscle with fibers at right angles to it, running up and in toward the ribs.
The deepest abdominal layer, with fibers running horizontally like a corset that you tighten when you brace or cough.
Latin for white line: a midline seam of tendon where the flank muscles' sheets meet, running from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis.
The only bone of the arm, running from shoulder to elbow. Hit its ulnar nerve groove and you get the funny bone feeling.
The smooth ball at the top of the arm bone that fits into the glenoid cavity of the scapula.
The bigger bump on the lateral side of the proximal humerus, where most rotator cuff muscles attach.
The smaller bump on the front of the proximal humerus, where subscapularis attaches. It sits medial to its larger partner.
A rough patch partway down the lateral shaft of the humerus, where the shoulder's big triangular muscle inserts.
The bump on the inner side of the distal humerus that you can feel at your elbow. The ulnar nerve runs right behind it.
The bump on the outer, thumb side of the distal humerus. Wrist extensors start here, which is why tennis elbow hurts there.
A spool-shaped surface on the medial distal humerus that the ulna wraps around. Its name is Latin for pulley.
The little round knob on the lateral distal humerus where the radius meets it. Its name means little head.
A deep pit on the back of the distal humerus that catches the tip of the ulna when you straighten your elbow.
The forearm bone on the pinky side. It forms the point of your elbow, and its big hook at the top locks onto the humerus.
The forearm bone on the thumb side. It rotates around its neighbor when you turn your palm up and down.
The point of your elbow: the big hook at the top of the ulna that you lean on.
The small lip on the front of the proximal ulna, below the trochlear notch. It fits into a matching fossa when you bend your elbow.
The C-shaped curve at the top of the ulna that grips the humerus like a wrench.
A disc at the top of the thumb-side forearm bone that spins against the capitulum and the ulna when you turn your hand.
A bump just below the neck of the radius, on its front side, where the biceps brachii tendon attaches.
The pointed tip at the distal end of the radius, on the thumb side of your wrist. You can feel it just above the thumb.
A sheet of tough connective tissue between the radius and ulna that holds them together and passes forces between them.
Eight small wrist bones in two rows. Try: Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle, proximal row from thumb side first.
The boat-shaped wrist bone on the thumb side of the proximal row, and the one most often broken when you fall on an outstretched hand.
A pea-shaped bone on the pinky side of the wrist that sits on top of the triquetrum. You can feel it at the base of your palm.
A distal-row wrist bone on the pinky side with a hook you can press in your palm. Hamulus means little hook.
The five bones of the palm, numbered 1 to 5 from the thumb. Their heads are your knuckles.
The finger bones: three in each finger and two in the thumb, for 14 in each hand.
The central space of the chest between the two lung cavities. It holds the heart, great vessels, trachea and esophagus.
The double-walled sac around the heart. Peri means around and cardia means heart.
The tough outermost layer of the heart's sac, made of dense connective tissue. It anchors the heart and keeps it from overfilling.
The thin layer lying right on the heart's surface. It is also the visceral layer of the serous sac, so it has two names.
The thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of cardiac muscle. Myo means muscle, and it does the pumping.
The smooth inner lining of the heart's chambers and valves, continuous with the lining of the blood vessels. Endo means within.
Receives oxygen-poor blood from both venae cavae and the coronary sinus. Right side, receiving chamber.
Pumps blood into the pulmonary trunk toward the lungs. Its wall is thinner than the left's because the lungs are close by.
Receives oxygen-rich blood from the four pulmonary veins. It sits at the back of the heart, closest to the esophagus.
The heart's strongest chamber, with the thickest wall, because it pumps blood out the aorta to the whole body. It forms the apex.
The thick muscular wall between the two lower chambers. Inter means between, septum means wall.
The valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, with three cusps. Try before you bi: three on the right comes before two on the left.
The left atrioventricular valve, with two cusps. Its shape reminded early anatomists of a bishop's mitre, hence the name.
The semilunar valve where blood leaves the right ventricle for the lungs. It sits at the base of the pulmonary trunk.
The semilunar valve where blood leaves the left ventricle for the body. The coronary arteries branch off just above it.
The heart strings: thin cords that tie the AV valve cusps to papillary muscles so the cusps can't flip back into the atria.
Cone-shaped muscles on the ventricle floor that pull the cords tight so the AV valves stay shut when the ventricles squeeze.
The big blue vessel leaving the right ventricle. It splits into the left and right pulmonary arteries headed for the lungs.
The body's largest artery, arching up and back from the left ventricle. Its arch gives off the vessels to the head and arms.
Brings oxygen-poor blood from the head, neck, arms and chest down into the right atrium. Superior means it enters from above.
The largest vein, carrying oxygen-poor blood from the legs and abdomen up into the right atrium.
The heart's own blood supply, branching from the aorta just above its valve. They are named for running around the heart like a crown.
A wide vein on the back of the heart in the groove between atria and ventricles. It drains the heart's own blood into the right atrium.
A hole between the atria in a fetus that lets blood skip the not-yet-working lungs. Foramen means opening.
The oval dent in the wall between the atria, left where the fetal opening sealed shut after birth. Fossa means shallow pit.
